title: Class 9 Maths, Chapter 4: Algebraic Identities, Step by Step
subtitle: For students who find maths hard. Every identity is shown as an area picture, a square or rectangle cut into pieces, so there is nothing to memorise blindly. Small steps, every line of algebra shown, practice with answers. Follows NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9 Part I, Chapter 4 (Exploring Algebraic Identities).

changelog.text: Linked into the Class 9 Maths Part I series: links to all chapters and to the chapters before and after this one.

First version: written for students who find maths hard. Algebra basics first, identities as area pictures, factorising with algebra tiles and the two-numbers method, practice in levels with answers, and a section for teachers and parents.

topics.label: Start here: the tools you need
topics.desc:
**Goal:** feel sure about four tools this chapter uses on every page: collecting like terms, squaring a term, opening one bracket, and multiplying two brackets.

If algebra has ever felt like a jumble of letters, spend time here. Everything later is built from these four moves.

links.label: Your textbook: NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9 Part I, Chapter 4 (free PDF)
DIKSHA: free NCERT videos and lessons

children.label: How to use this roadmap
children.desc:
- Go in order. Each step is small. On the map the steps go left and right, so press **Checklist view** at the top to see them as a list, in order.
- Click a box to open it. Read the idea, follow the worked example, then do **Your turn**.
- Write your answer in your notebook **before** you open the answer box.
- Got it wrong? That is fine. Read the answer, then try the next one.
- When a step feels easy, mark it **Done**. Your progress is saved on this device.

**One idea runs through this whole chapter: an identity is a picture of an area.** A square or rectangle is cut into pieces. Adding up the pieces gives the same area as the whole. Every rule in this chapter comes from a picture like that.

links.label: All eight chapters: Class 9 Maths, Part I
Previous chapter: 3. The World of Numbers

children.label: Check yourself (2 minutes)
children.desc: Four quick questions. Write your answers first, then open each box. If you get one wrong, do the step named in the answer.

children.label: Like terms
children.desc:
**Like terms** have exactly the same letters with the same powers. Only like terms can be added.

- 3x and 5x are like terms: 3x + 5x = 8x.
- 2x² and 7x² are like terms: 2x² + 7x² = 9x².
- 3x and 3x² are **not** like terms. You can't add them. Leave them as 3x + 3x².
- xy and yx are like terms, because x × y = y × x.

**Worked example:** 4x + 3 − x + 6 = 3x + 9. The x terms go together (4x − x = 3x). The numbers go together (3 + 6 = 9).

faq.q: Your turn: simplify 2a + 7 + 5a − 3, and x² + 3x + 2x² − x.

children.label: Squaring a term
children.desc:
**Squaring** means multiplying a thing by itself. x² means x × x.

When a term has a number **and** a letter, square **both**:
- (3x)² = 3x × 3x = **9x²**, not 3x².
- (5y)² = 5y × 5y = **25y²**.
- (2xy)² = 2xy × 2xy = **4x²y²**.

**Signs:** a negative times a negative is positive. So (−4)² = 16 and (−3x)² = 9x².

**Cubing** means three times: (2x)³ = 2x × 2x × 2x = **8x³**.

children.label: Opening one bracket
children.desc:
The number outside multiplies **everything** inside. This is the **distributive** rule.

- 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12
- x(x + 5) = x² + 5x
- −2(x − 5) = −2x + 10. Careful: −2 × −5 = +10.

The most common mistake is to multiply only the first term: 3(x + 4) is **not** 3x + 4.

links.label: Math is Fun: the distributive law

children.label: Multiplying two brackets
children.desc:
Every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second. A **grid** keeps you from missing one.

**Worked example: (2x + 3)(x + 4).**
- Write 2x and +3 across the top. Write x and +4 down the side.
- Fill each box: 2x × x = 2x², 3 × x = 3x, 2x × 4 = 8x, 3 × 4 = 12.
- Add the boxes and collect like terms: **(2x + 3)(x + 4) = 2x² + 3x + 8x + 12 = 2x² + 11x + 12**.

Four boxes, four products, every time. Use the grid until you don't need it.

images.caption: The grid method: one box for each pair of terms

topics.label: What is an identity?
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know the difference between an equation and an identity, and how to test one with numbers.

This is the word in the chapter's title. It is a simple idea once you see it.

children.label: Equation or identity?
children.desc:
An **equation** is true for only some values of the letter.
- x + 3 = 7 is true only when x = 4.

An **identity** is true for **every** value of the letters.
- 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 is true for x = 0, x = 1, x = 100, x = −5 ... every number.

An identity is really a **shortcut you can always trust**. That is why they are worth learning.

links.label: Math is Fun: what is an identity?

faq.q: Your turn: equation or identity? (a) 3x = 12, (b) x + x = 2x, (c) x² = 9.
faq.a: (a) **Equation**: only x = 4 works. (b) **Identity**: always true. (c) **Equation**: only x = 3 or x = −3 work.

children.label: Testing an identity with numbers
children.desc:
You can check any rule by putting numbers in.

**Worked example:** is (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² true? Try a = 5, b = 2.
- Left: (5 + 2)(5 − 2) = 7 × 3 = 21.
- Right: 25 − 4 = 21. **Same.**

Numbers can **catch a false rule** with just one failure. But a few successes do not **prove** a rule. Proof comes from algebra or a picture, which is what the next milestones do.

faq.q: Your turn: test (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² with a = 3, b = 4.
Your turn: test the same rule with a = −2, b = 5.
faq.a: Left: 3² = **9**. Right: 4 + 2(−2)(5) + 25 = 4 − 20 + 25 = **9**. Same. It works for negatives too.

children.label: The biggest trap in this chapter
children.desc:
**(a + b)² is NOT a² + b².** Check with a = 3, b = 4:
- (3 + 4)² = 7² = **49**.
- 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = **25**.

25 is short by 24. That missing piece is **2ab** = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24. The next milestone shows exactly where it hides.

If you remember only one thing from this chapter, remember this.

faq.q: Your turn: show that (5 + 1)² is not 5² + 1². What is missing?

children.label: A pattern to puzzle over
children.desc:
Take three square numbers in a row, like 4, 9, 16. Add the first and last: 4 + 16 = 20. Take away twice the middle: 20 − 18 = **2**.

Try 25, 36, 49: 25 + 49 − 72 = **2**. Try 100, 121, 144: 244 − 242 = **2**.

Always 2. Why? Keep it in mind. The answer is in *Why the puzzle always gives 2*, two milestones from here.

topics.label: Squaring a sum: (a + b)²
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² from a picture, say it in words, and use it on terms and on numbers.

This is the first and most used identity. Exercise Set 4.1 uses it.

children.label: The picture: one square, four pieces
children.desc:
Draw a square with side **a + b**. Its area is (a + b)².

Now cut it along the a and b marks. You get four pieces:
- one big square, area **a²**
- one small square, area **b²**
- **two** rectangles, each a × b, area **ab** each.

Add the pieces: **(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²**.

Now the trap makes sense. a² + b² forgets the two rectangles.

links.label: Math is Fun: special binomial products

faq.q: Your turn: draw a square of side 5 + 2 on squared paper. What are the areas of the four pieces?

images.caption: A square of side a + b cut into four pieces

children.label: Say it in words
children.desc:
Learn the rule as a sentence, not just letters:

**First squared, plus twice first times second, plus second squared.**

Then a and b can be anything.

**Worked example: (x + 3)².** First is x, second is 3.
- First squared: x².
- Twice first times second: 2 × x × 3 = 6x.
- Second squared: 9.
- So **(x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9**.

children.label: When the terms have numbers in front
children.desc:
Put brackets round each term first, so you square the whole term.

**Worked example: (3x + 2y)².** First is 3x, second is 2y.
- First squared: (3x)² = 9x².
- Twice first times second: 2 × 3x × 2y = 12xy.
- Second squared: (2y)² = 4y².
- So **(3x + 2y)² = 9x² + 12xy + 4y²**.

Fractions work the same way: (x + 1/2)² = x² + 2 × x × 1/2 + 1/4 = **x² + x + 1/4**.

faq.a: First squared: x²/9. Twice first times second: 2 × x/3 × 3 = 2x. Second squared: 9. So **x²/9 + 2x + 9**.

children.label: Squaring numbers in your head
children.desc:
Split the number into a round part and a small part.

**Worked example: 51².**
- 51² = (50 + 1)² = 2500 + 100 + 1 = 2601.
- That is 50², then 2 × 50 × 1, then 1².

**Another: 103²** = (100 + 3)² = 10000 + 600 + 9 = **10609**.

topics.label: Squaring a difference: (a − b)²
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², and see that only one sign changed.

If you know the last milestone, this one is nearly free. Exercise Set 4.2 uses it.

children.label: Only the middle sign changes
children.desc:
**(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²**

Compare with (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². The squares are still **plus**. Only the middle term turns **minus**.

Why the last term is plus: b² comes from (−b) × (−b), and minus times minus is plus.

**Worked example: (x − 4)².**
- First squared: x².
- Twice first times second, with a minus: −2 × x × 4 = −8x.
- Second squared: 16.
- So **(x − 4)² = x² − 8x + 16**.

links.label: Math is Fun: special binomial products

children.label: The picture: cutting off two strips
children.desc:
Start with a big square of side **a**. Area a².

The blue square in the corner has side **a − b**. To get it, cut off two strips.
- Each strip, including the corner, is a by b. Take both away: a² − 2ab.
- But the little corner square b² was inside **both** strips. It was taken away twice, so add it back once.

Result: **(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²**.

images.caption: Inside a square of side a, the corner square has side a − b

children.label: Squaring numbers just below a round one
children.desc:
Numbers like 29, 98 or 199 are just below a round number. Use the minus rule.

**Worked example: 29².**
- 29² = (30 − 1)² = 900 − 60 + 1 = 841.
- That is 30², then take 2 × 30 × 1, then add 1².

**Another: 98²** = (100 − 2)² = 10000 − 400 + 4 = **9604**.

children.label: Why the puzzle always gives 2
children.desc:
Call the middle number n. The numbers in a row are n − 1, n, n + 1.
- (n − 1)² = n² − 2n + 1
- (n + 1)² = n² + 2n + 1
- Add them: 2n² + 2. The −2n and +2n cancel.
- Take away twice the middle square, 2n²: you are left with **2**.

So it is 2 for **every** n. Trying numbers suggested the pattern. Algebra proved it.

faq.q: Your turn: what do you get from 4 squares in a row? Try 1, 4, 9, 16 with first + last − middle two.
faq.a: 1 + 16 − 4 − 9 = **4**. Try 4, 9, 16, 25: 29 − 25 = **4** again. With algebra: n², (n+1)², (n+2)², (n+3)² gives first + last − middle two = 4 every time.

topics.label: Difference of two squares
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b², and use it for quick products.

This is the friendliest identity in the chapter: the middle terms disappear.

children.label: The middle terms cancel
children.desc:
Multiply (a + b)(a − b) with a grid:
- a × a = a², a × (−b) = −ab, b × a = +ab, b × (−b) = −b².
- The −ab and +ab cancel.
- So **(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²**.

**Worked example:** (x + 5)(x − 5) = x² − 25.

Spot it: the two brackets are the **same** except for one sign.

links.label: Math is Fun: special binomial products

children.label: The picture: cut the corner, move a piece
children.desc:
Take a square of side a and cut a small square b² out of the corner. What is left, a² − b², is an L shape.

Cut the L into two rectangles, A and B. Turn A on its side and put B next to it. You get one long rectangle.
- Its length is **a + b**.
- Its height is **a − b**.

Same area, so **a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)**.

images.caption: Cut the corner out, rearrange the L into one rectangle

children.label: Quick products
children.desc:
When two numbers sit the same distance either side of a round number, use this rule.

**Worked example: 31 × 29.** Both are 1 away from 30.
- 31 × 29 = (30 + 1)(30 − 1) = 900 − 1 = **899**.

**Another: 102 × 98** = (100 + 2)(100 − 2) = 10000 − 4 = **9996**.

children.label: An old trick: squares that end in 5
children.desc:
Around 750 CE, **Śrīdharāchārya** used this identity in the form a² = (a + b)(a − b) + b² to square numbers fast.

**Worked example: 45².** Take b = 5.
- 45² = (45 + 5)(45 − 5) + 25 = 50 × 40 + 25 = 2000 + 25 = **2025**.

The trick always lands on easy round numbers when the number ends in 5.

topics.label: Factorising: running the rules backwards
topics.desc:
**Goal:** turn an expression back into brackets, using a common factor, a perfect square or a difference of squares.

Expanding opens brackets. **Factorising** puts them back. Same identities, read from right to left. Exercise Set 4.2 starts here.

children.label: What factorising means
children.desc:
With numbers, **factorising** means writing a number as a product: 12 = 3 × 4.

With algebra it is the same: write an expression as things multiplied together.
- Expanding: (x + 3)² → x² + 6x + 9.
- Factorising: x² + 6x + 9 → (x + 3)².

**Always check** a factorisation by expanding it again. If you get back where you started, it is right.

links.label: Math is Fun: factoring in algebra

children.label: Step 1, always: take out a common factor
children.desc:
Before anything else, look for a number or letter that divides **every** term.

- 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)
- x² + 5x = x(x + 5)
- 2x² − 18 = 2(x² − 9), and then x² − 9 can be factorised again (next steps).

Taking out the common factor first makes the rest much easier to see.

faq.q: Your turn: take out the common factor: 4x + 20, 7a − 14b, y² − 3y.

children.label: Spotting a perfect square
children.desc:
An expression is a perfect square if it passes **three checks**:
- Is the **first** term a square? Find what was squared.
- Is the **last** term a square? Find what was squared.
- Is the **middle** term **twice** those two multiplied?

**Worked example: 4x² + 12x + 9.**
- 4x² = (2x)². Yes.
- 9 = 3². Yes.
- 2 × 2x × 3 = 12x. Yes, it matches the middle.
- So **4x² + 12x + 9 = (2x + 3)²**.

If the middle term is **minus**, use a minus: x² − 10x + 25 = (x − 5)².

faq.q: Your turn (harder): factorise 3x² + 12x + 12. Hint: step 1 first.

children.label: Factorising a difference of squares
children.desc:
Look for **two squares with a minus between them**, and nothing else.

**Worked example: 9x² − 16.**
- 9x² = (3x)² and 16 = 4².
- So **9x² − 16 = (3x + 4)(3x − 4)**.

Back to the earlier one: 2x² − 18 = 2(x + 3)(x − 3).

Warning: x² **+** 16 can't be done this way. It needs a minus.

faq.q: Your turn: factorise x² − 49, 25 − y² and 4a² − 81b².

topics.label: Factorising x² + bx + c
topics.desc:
**Goal:** factorise expressions like x² + 7x + 12 by finding two numbers, first with algebra tiles, then without.

This is the most useful skill in the chapter, and the one most students find hardest. Go slowly. Exercise Set 4.4 uses it.

children.label: Algebra tiles: making a rectangle
children.desc:
**Algebra tiles** are pieces of card. A big square is x², a long strip is x, and a small square is 1.

To factorise x² + 5x + 6, take 1 big square, 5 strips and 6 small squares. Then arrange them into **one rectangle**.

- Put the x² in the corner.
- Put 3 strips on the right, 2 strips below.
- The 6 small squares fill the gap as a 2 by 3 block.
- Now read the sides: **x + 3** across and **x + 2** down.

So **x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3)**. You can cut tiles from card and try this yourself.

faq.q: Your turn: which rectangle do x² + 4x + 3 tiles make?
faq.a: 3 small squares only fit as a 1 by 3 block, so the strips split 1 and 3. Sides x + 1 and x + 3: x² + 4x + 3 = (x + 1)(x + 3).

images.caption: The three kinds of algebra tile

children.label: Without tiles: find two numbers
children.desc:
Look at what (x + p)(x + q) gives:
- (x + p)(x + q) = x² + (p + q)x + pq
- The middle number is p + q (they **add**).
- The last number is p × q (they **multiply**).

So to factorise x² + 7x + 12, find **two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7**.

List the pairs that multiply to 12, and check their sum:
- 1 and 12: sum 13. No.
- 2 and 6: sum 8. No.
- 3 and 4: sum **7**. Yes!

So **x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)**. Check by expanding.

faq.q: Your turn: factorise x² + 6x + 8 and x² + 9x + 20.

children.label: When there are minus signs
children.desc:
Use the **last** sign to decide, then the **middle** sign:
- Last is **plus**: both numbers have the **same** sign as the middle term.
- Last is **minus**: the numbers have **opposite** signs. The bigger one takes the sign of the middle term.

**Worked example 1:** x² − 7x + 10. Multiply to +10, add to −7. Both minus: −2 and −5. So **x² − 7x + 10 = (x − 2)(x − 5)**.

**Worked example 2:** x² + 2x − 15. Multiply to −15, add to +2. Opposite signs, bigger one plus: +5 and −3. So **x² + 2x − 15 = (x + 5)(x − 3)**.

faq.q: Your turn: factorise x² − 8x + 15 and x² − x − 12.
faq.a: x² − 8x + 15 = (x − 3)(x − 5). For x² − x − 12: multiply to −12, add to −1, so −4 and +3: x² − x − 12 = (x − 4)(x + 3).

faq.q: Your turn: factorise y² + 3y − 28 and a² − 12a + 36.

children.label: When x² has a number in front
children.desc:
For 2x² + 7x + 3, use **split the middle**:
- Multiply the first and last numbers: 2 × 3 = **6**.
- Find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 7: **1 and 6**.
- Split the middle: 2x² + x + 6x + 3.
- Group in pairs and take out a factor from each: x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1).
- Both have (2x + 1), so take it out.

So **2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3)**. Check by expanding with a grid.

topics.label: Three terms and cubes
topics.desc:
**Goal:** square three terms, and cube two. These are the same picture idea, made bigger.

Do this milestone after the earlier ones feel comfortable. Exercise Set 4.3 and the end-of-chapter exercises use it.

children.label: Squaring three terms: (a + b + c)²
children.desc:
Cut a square of side a + b + c into a 3 by 3 grid. There are **3 squares** and **6 rectangles**, and each rectangle appears **twice**.

**(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca**

In words: square each term, then add twice every pair.

**Worked example: (x + 2y + 3)².**
- Squares: x², 4y², 9.
- Twice each pair: 2 × x × 2y = 4xy, 2 × 2y × 3 = 12y, 2 × 3 × x = 6x.
- So **(x + 2y + 3)² = x² + 4y² + 9 + 4xy + 12y + 6x**.

faq.q: Your turn (harder): expand (x − y + 2z)². Careful with signs.
faq.a: Squares: x², y², 4z². Pairs: 2(x)(−y) = −2xy, 2(−y)(2z) = −4yz, 2(2z)(x) = 4xz. So (x − y + 2z)² = x² + y² + 4z² − 2xy − 4yz + 4xz.

images.caption: A square of side a + b + c: 3 squares and 6 rectangles

children.label: Cubing a sum: (a + b)³
children.desc:
A cube of edge a + b can be cut into 8 blocks: a cube a³, a cube b³, three blocks a × a × b, and three blocks a × b × b.

**(a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³**

You can also get it by multiplying (a + b) by (a + b)², which you already know.

**Worked example: (x + 2)³.**
- a = x, b = 2.
- x³ + 3 × x² × 2 + 3 × x × 4 + 8.
- So **(x + 2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8**.

The numbers 1, 3, 3, 1 are the pattern to remember.

links.label: Math is Fun: binomial theorem (for the curious)

faq.q: Your turn: expand (y + 1)³ and find 11³ with the rule.

children.label: Cubing a difference: (a − b)³
children.desc:
Swap b for −b in the last rule. The signs now **alternate**: plus, minus, plus, minus.

**(a − b)³ = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³**

**Worked example: (x − 3)³** = x³ − 9x² + 27x − 27.

**With numbers: 19³** = (20 − 1)³ = 8000 − 1200 + 60 − 1 = **6859**.

children.label: Sums and differences of cubes
children.desc:
Two more identities, mostly used for factorising:
- **a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)**
- **a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)**

A memory aid: the first bracket has the **same** sign as the question. The second bracket starts with the **opposite** sign.

**Worked example:** x³ − 8 = x³ − 2³, so x³ − 8 = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4).

Check it with x = 3: 27 − 8 = 19, and (1)(9 + 6 + 4) = 19.

topics.label: Using factorising
topics.desc:
**Goal:** use factorising to simplify fractions with algebra in them, and to solve real problems about areas.

This is where all the factorising pays off. Exercise Set 4.5 and the end-of-chapter word problems use it.

children.label: Simplifying algebraic fractions
children.desc:
Cancel works the same as with numbers: 6/8 = (2 × 3)/(2 × 4) = 3/4. You can only cancel a **factor**, something that **multiplies** the whole top and the whole bottom.

**Worked example: (x² − 9) / (x² + 5x + 6).**
- Factorise the top: (x + 3)(x − 3).
- Factorise the bottom: (x + 2)(x + 3).
- Both have (x + 3). Cancel it.
- Answer: **(x − 3)/(x + 2)**.

**The big mistake:** in (x + 3)/x you can't cancel the x's, because x is not a factor of the whole top. Try x = 1: (1 + 3)/1 = 4, not 3.

children.label: Finding the sides of a rectangle
children.desc:
If you know the **area** of a rectangle as an expression, factorising gives the **sides**.

**Worked example:** Meena makes a rectangle from 1 big x² tile, 6 strips and 8 small squares. What are its sides?
- Area = x² + 6x + 8.
- Multiply to 8, add to 6: 2 and 4.
- x² + 6x + 8 = (x + 2)(x + 4).
- So the sides are **x + 2** and **x + 4**.

faq.q: Your turn: a rectangle has area x² + 10x + 21. Find its sides.
faq.a: Multiply to 21, add to 10: 3 and 7. x² + 10x + 21 = (x + 3)(x + 7). Sides **x + 3** and **x + 7**.

faq.q: Your turn: a rectangle has area 4a² − 9b². Find possible sides.

children.label: Solving a problem by factorising
children.desc:
If two numbers multiply to **zero**, one of them must be zero. That lets us solve.

**Worked example:** a garden is 3 m longer than it is wide. Its area is 40 m². How wide is it?
- Let the width be x. The length is x + 3.
- Area: x(x + 3) = 40, so x² + 3x − 40 = 0.
- Multiply to −40, add to 3: +8 and −5. So (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0.
- Either x = −8 or x = 5. A width can't be negative, so **x = 5**.
- Width **5 m**, length **8 m**. Check: 5 × 8 = 40.

faq.q: Your turn: a rectangle is 2 cm longer than it is wide, and its area is 48 cm². Find its sides.
faq.a: x(x + 2) = 48, so x² + 2x − 48 = 0. Multiply to −48, add to 2: +8 and −6. (x + 8)(x − 6) = 0, so x = 6. Sides **6 cm and 8 cm**.

faq.q: Your turn (harder): a square park has side 30 m. A path of width p metres is built all round the outside. Find the area of the path.
faq.a: The big square has side 30 + 2p. Path area = (30 + 2p)² − 30² = 900 + 120p + 4p² − 900 = **4p² + 120p** square metres.

topics.label: When you're ready: challenge questions
topics.desc: **For later.** These match the starred (challenge) and harder end-of-chapter questions in your textbook. Come here only after the earlier milestones feel comfortable. It is completely fine to skip this milestone the first time through.

children.label: Why n³ − n is always divisible by 6
children.desc:
Factorise: n³ − n = n(n² − 1) = **(n − 1) × n × (n + 1)**.

That is **three whole numbers in a row** multiplied together.
- In any two numbers in a row, one is even. So the product divides by 2.
- In any three numbers in a row, one is a multiple of 3. So it divides by 3.
- Divisible by 2 and by 3 means divisible by **6**.

Check: n = 5 gives 125 − 5 = 120 = 4 × 5 × 6 = 6 × 20.

children.label: x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz
children.desc:
One more identity, for three letters:

**x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx)**

**Worked example:** three numbers add to 6. Their pairs multiplied add to 11 (xy + yz + zx = 11). Their product is 6. Find the sum of their cubes.
- First find x² + y² + z² from (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2(xy + yz + zx): 36 = x² + y² + z² + 22, so x² + y² + z² = 14.
- Then x³ + y³ + z³ − 3 × 6 = 6 × (14 − 11) = 18.
- So x³ + y³ + z³ = 18 + 18 = **36**.

(The numbers are 1, 2 and 3, and 1 + 8 + 27 = 36. It works.)

faq.q: Your turn: if a + b + c = 4 and ab + bc + ca = 5, find a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc.

children.label: A number plus its reciprocal
children.desc:
**Worked example:** a number plus 1 over that number is 5/2. Find the number.
- x + 1/x = 5/2. Multiply everything by 2x: 2x² + 2 = 5x.
- So 2x² − 5x + 2 = 0.
- Split the middle (2 × 2 = 4; multiply to 4, add to −5: −1 and −4): 2x² − x − 4x + 2 = x(2x − 1) − 2(2x − 1) = (2x − 1)(x − 2).
- So x = **2** or x = **1/2**. Check: 2 + 1/2 = 5/2.

children.label: Is it an identity?
children.desc:
Decide by expanding both sides.

**Worked example:** is (a + b)² − (a − b)² = 4ab?
- (a² + 2ab + b²) − (a² − 2ab + b²) = 4ab. **Yes.** The squares cancel; the middles add.

Use it as a trick: 4 × 7 × 3 = 10² − 4² = 100 − 16 = 84.

faq.q: Your turn: is (x + 1)² = x² + 1 an identity?
faq.a: **No.** (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1. The two sides agree only when 2x = 0, so only for x = 0. That makes it an equation, not an identity.

topics.label: For teachers and parents
topics.desc:
**For the adults helping.** Students can skip this milestone.

This chapter introduces about ten identities, which can feel like a list to memorise. For a student who finds maths hard, it isn't one. The roadmap treats every identity as **an area picture**: a square or rectangle cut into pieces. The core path is the three square identities, the difference of squares, and factorising x² + bx + c. Cubes, the three-letter identity and the proofs are kept for later.

children.label: How to help a student who is struggling
children.desc:
- **Start with *Check yourself*.** Most trouble in this chapter is really trouble with like terms, squaring a term like 3x, or multiplying two brackets.
- **Use the grid method** for every product until it is automatic. It removes the 'which terms did I multiply?' problem.
- **Make algebra tiles** from card (x² squares, x strips, unit squares). Building the rectangle for x² + 5x + 6 makes factorising concrete.
- **Test with numbers.** Whenever a student writes (a + b)² = a² + b², ask them to try a = 3, b = 4. One check convinces more than any explanation.
- **Say the rules in words:** 'first squared, twice first times second, second squared.'
- **Always check a factorisation by expanding.** It turns guessing into checking.

children.label: A 10-period plan, with activities
children.desc:
- **Period 1:** the *Start here* tools: like terms, squaring a term, one bracket, two brackets with the grid.
- **Period 2:** equations vs identities; testing with numbers; the (a + b)² ≠ a² + b² trap. **Activity:** the 'always 2' puzzle with consecutive squares.
- **Period 3:** (a + b)² from a cut square; in words; with terms; squaring numbers (Exercise Set 4.1). **Activity:** cut a paper square of side 7 into 5 + 2 pieces.
- **Period 4:** (a − b)² and squaring numbers like 29²; why the puzzle gives 2.
- **Period 5:** difference of two squares with the cut-and-move picture; quick products. **Activity:** cut the L shape and rearrange it.
- **Period 6:** factorising: common factor, perfect squares, difference of squares (Exercise Set 4.2).
- **Period 7:** algebra tiles, then 'two numbers that multiply and add'. **Activity:** card tiles in pairs.
- **Period 8:** signs; x² with a number in front (Exercise Set 4.4).
- **Period 9:** (a + b + c)², cubes (Exercise Set 4.3); simplifying algebraic fractions (Exercise Set 4.5).
- **Period 10:** area word problems; exit ticket. Challenge questions for those ready.

children.label: Mistakes to watch for
children.desc:
- (a + b)² = a² + b², forgetting 2ab.
- (3x)² = 3x² instead of 9x².
- (a − b)² = a² − b², or a² − 2ab − b².
- 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4: multiplying only the first term.
- In x² + bx + c, choosing numbers that **add** to c and **multiply** to b (the wrong way round).
- Sign errors when the last term is negative.
- Not taking out the common factor first, then getting stuck.
- Cancelling terms instead of factors: (x + 3)/x = 3.
- Trying to factorise x² + 16 as a difference of squares.
- Keeping a negative length when solving an area problem.
